meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Our patience will achieve more than our force'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Edmund Burke — from Reflections on the Revolution in France, published November 1790. Verified against the text and a 1790 scan.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The sentence appears in Burke’s Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in London in November 1790, in the passage where he argues that constitutions must be reformed slowly, by many minds working together, rather than remade at speed. A 1790 printing scanned by the Internet Archive carries it in the period spelling: “Our patience will atchieve more than our force.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Reflections on the Revolution in France, and on the Proceedings in Certain Societies in London Relative to That Event
November 1790 · London, printed for James Dodsley of Pall Mall
A pamphlet written as a letter “intended to have been sent to a gentleman in Paris”
“Our patience will atchieve more than our force.”

source.excerpt: Political arrangement, as it is a work for social ends, is to be only wrought by social means. There mind must conspire with mind. Time is required to produce that union of minds which alone can produce all the good we aim at. Our patience will achieve more than our force.
trail: Searched the full text of Project Gutenberg’s The Works of the Right Honourable Edmund Burke, Vol. III ↗, which contains Reflections on the Revolution in France; the sentence is there, in the passage on reforming slowly.
Confirmed the same passage, word for word, in the independent Wikisource transcription of the work ↗.
Checked a period witness: a 1790 printing scanned by the Internet Archive ↗ carries it on page 249 as “Our patience will atchieve more than our force.”

Cross-checked Wikiquote’s Edmund Burke page ↗, which lists the line under Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) rather than among its misattributed or unsourced entries. Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation.

author.name: Edmund Burke
author.heading: Who was Edmund Burke?
author.metaLine: 1729–1797 · Anglo-Irish statesman, orator and political philosopher
author.bio: Edmund Burke was an Anglo-Irish writer and politician who sat in the British House of Commons as a Whig and is widely credited as the founder of modern conservative political philosophy. He made his name defending the American colonists and prosecuting the East India Company’s Warren Hastings, then broke with many of his own allies over the French Revolution. Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) is the book that argument produced — and the book this sentence comes from.

misattribution.heading: The quote is real — the citations around it are not
misattribution.intro: Burke is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for invented quotations, so a Burke line that turns out to be genuine is worth saying plainly: this one is in the book. What goes wrong with it is smaller — the wording gets trimmed and the source gets dropped.

items.why: A shortened form circulates widely — The Foundation for a Better Life, for instance, publishes it as “Patience will achieve more than force” ↗ with no work cited. Burke’s sentence has the possessives: our patience, our force.
Typical of the genre: The Quotations Page gives the line and Burke’s dates but cites only a motivational-quotations compilation ↗, not the book — leaving readers no way to check it.

By contrast, the sentence most often hung on Burke is fake: Wikiquote lists “All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing” as misattributed ↗, noting it has no definite original source and closely resembles a remark John Stuart Mill made in an 1867 address at the University of St Andrews.

misattribution.truthLine: The real sentence, in its real setting, is on the page: “Time is required to produce that union of minds which alone can produce all the good we aim at. Our patience will achieve more than our force.” ↗

context.heading: Why Burke wrote it
lead: Reflections on the Revolution in France was published in London in November 1790 by James Dodsley, cast as a letter to a gentleman in Paris — it grew out of Burke’s replies to the young French aristocrat Charles-Jean-François Depont, who had written asking what he made of events across the Channel. Burke’s answer was not what a sympathiser wanted to hear: he argued for gradual, constitutional reform rather than revolution, and warned that doctrines built on abstractions could be turned to justify tyranny.

The line sits inside that argument, not beside it. Burke has just imagined an objection — that reforming slowly “is not fit for an Assembly which glories in performing in a few months the work of ages” — and answers that political arrangements are social work, requiring many minds and therefore time. Patience is not passivity here; it is the method.
detailsBody: It sold. Wikipedia’s account of the work records that thirteen thousand copies were purchased in the first five weeks, and that by the following September it had gone through eleven editions — which is why so many separate 1790 and 1791 printings of the book survive in library scans today.

That multiplicity of printings is also why the modern quotation looks slightly different from the page. Eighteenth-century compositors set the word as atchieve; later collected editions of Burke’s Works modernised it to achieve, and that is the form every quote site now reproduces.
